label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
To: timeline
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: none

Spent the last two Saturdays redoing a shed out in Brookline. I'm a union electrician and I've seen a lot of bad work, but this one was special. I wrote down everything we found so I wouldn't forget any of it.

When I opened the panel, my wife was standing right there and goes, "Who's Ron?" Like I'd know.

Here's the junk list:

- Power came from three orange extension cords daisy chained out the basement window, across the yard, and under the deck. A jungle gym for fires.
- One splice wrapped in duct tape. Not electrical tape. Duct tape.
- A 30 amp breaker protecting 14 gauge wire. The breaker was more of a suggestion.
- The outlet in the shed was wired with speaker wire. It did not play music, or at least not the way it was supposed to.
- The "GFCI" outlet was a regular outlet with a GFCI sticker on it. Honest mistake? No. Sticker.
- The ceiling fan box was held up by one drywall screw. Ceiling fan, spinning over somebody's head.
- A mouse nest in the junction box. The mice were fine. Unbothered. Honestly the most relaxed thing in the whole job.
- Inside the panel door, in Sharpie: SHED - DON'T TOUCH - RON.

Ron, if you're out there, we did not touch it. We fixed it.

What we did: trenched 18 inches down, ran proper 12/2 UF, put in a 20 amp GFCI breaker, real box, real outlets, and got the fan on a proper brace. Two Saturdays. Payment was two pizzas and a case of Yuengling, which was more than the job was worth to whoever did it the first time.

Now the serious part, because I'm not just laughing. Stuff like this burns houses down. Extension cords under a deck, tape splices, breakers that don't match the wire. Those are fires waiting for a Saturday night. The guy who did this wasn't evil. He was cheap and a little proud, and honestly that's most of the bad wiring I've ever seen. Nobody sets out to start a fire. They just don't want to pay for it the right way.

If you have a shed, garage, basement, or anything with power you're not sure about, call a licensed electrician. Not your buddy. Not a guy with a YouTube video and a good attitude. Licensed, insured, pulls permits. It costs more up front and a lot less than a fire.

And push the test button on your GFCIs. If it doesn't click off, it's not a GFCI, no matter what the sticker says.
